KK005-004----:
On the steep W-facing slope of an N-S hill, rising from 220m to over 300m over a distance of c. 300m. The top of the monument is on the crest of the hill. It falls gently to W initially (for c. 11m), drops (H 0.35m) and flattens out slightly on a natural terrace (for c. 5m) before falling steeply down slope to the base of the hill. In upland meadow. There are panoramic views S-W-N, with a very good view to the NE but only from the very top of the monument. Identified as a possible monument in 1955, this consists of two low earthen banks (L c. 310m), running roughly parallel downslope. The cursus terminates at the crest of the hill with a curving terminal bank (Wth 3.6m; overall Wth 8m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.13m). In the upper portion, a profile across the monuments provides measures as follows, bank to N (Wth 2m; overall Wth 4.8m; ext. H 0.4m; int. H 0.65m), interior (Wth 13m), bank to S (Wth 2m; overall Wth 7m; ext. H 0.2m; int. H 0.75m).The banks appear to have a high concentration of stone, possibly stone-walling overgrown with grass sod. The stone is a local shale. The interior of the cursus is lower than the exterior. At the E end of the monument the banks are 7.7m apart, running westward, the monument widens as it runs down the slope, just above the first field boundary the banks are 20m apart. In the lower field it is not possible to trace the banks of the cursus, they may be incorporated in one or both of the field boundaries. The orientation of the cursus changes from W-facing at the top (L c. 125m) to WSW-facing (L c. 100m) and possibly back to W-facing, though it may continue WSW to the end. The banks are an overall width of c. 8-10m in the lower grassy field.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 12 June 2017
KK008-109----:
At one of the lowest points immediately below a gravel ridge, in generally flat terrain, in grassland. A mound of earth and stone (dims. 9.5m N-S; 6m E-W; H 1.2m at E; H 0.1m at W) which is covered by a number of large boulders, some of which appear to be in situ. The monument is partially truncated, especially at the S.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 17 January 2018
KK008-124001-:
On the summit of Mount Garret hill (349m), at the centre of a hillfort (KK008-124001-). It consists of a ruined cairn (diam. c. 25m; H 1-2m). Six kerb-stones are exposed along the W side. The monument was investigated by Graves in 1851 and was found to contain a central chamber (L c. 2m; Wth 1.35m; D 1m) (Graves 1849-51, vol. 1, 289-92). Its E side was formed of four 'immense stones, averaging six feet long [1.83m], and from two feet six to three feet wide [0.76-0.91m], piled one on the other'. The W side was of similar construction and was formed of five slabs. The S end was closed by a large slab set on edge. The N extremity was built up with smaller stones 'without any order or regularity'. It appears to have been roofed by two flags 'each about five feet long [1.52m], and between three and four feet wide [0.9m-1.22m]' which were displaced and lay in the chamber. The fill of the chamber contained two adult human skeletons, apparently extended; their heads lay to the S. Some 2m S of this chamber and on a much higher level in the cairn was a small cist. In it were found cremated bone and sherds of pottery with 'indented herring-bone or zig-zag pattern', probably from an urn or food vessel (ibid.). Both the cist and S end stone of the central chamber are still visible. Ryan (1981, 144) has suggested that this monument may be a probable Linkardstown-type burial. The occurrence of a central megalithic chamber in a kerbed, round cairn together with the hilltop siting of the monument, however, could indicate links with the passage-tomb tradition.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 23 January 2018
KK008-140----:
The OS Letters (1839) refer to the southern ringfort (KK008-042----) in the townland of Rathosheen, which, 'is said to have been the burial place of that Hero-Bard. His grave was marked in it by two upright stones at several years distance but the place was dug up several years ago by money dreamers and the stones carried away by some wicked man who had not the fear of Oisinn or the fairies before his eyes, but he died since, tho' not very old! I could wish he had gone before he disturbed my old friends bones. Nothing remains now to mark the grave but a circular hollow in the south western part of the Rath' (O’Flanagan (ed.) 1930, 118-19 (40)). Being located within a ringfort these cannot be prehistoric standing stones, unless the enclosure is not a ringfort. However, as standing stones most accurately reflects what is described in the OS letters, the classification has been retained.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 23 January 2018
KK012-062----:
On the crest of a N-S ridge, with land sloping gently away to the E and W down to the river plains, in tillage. There are very good views in all directions. Formerly in the demesne of Borrismore House, it is described by Carrigan (1905, vol. 2, 366) as, 'a cromlech in Mr. De Courcy's land in Borrismore'. A large roofstone-like stone (L 2.9m; Wth 2.2m; T 1.1m thick, partly rests on two inclined blocks. The E stone (dims. 2.2m x 1m; T 1m) leans to the S. The W stone (L 1.4m; T 0.6m) leans to the W. If erect it would be 1.7m high. A tree grows at the N foot of the monument. Two smaller slabs lie beside it and field clearance has been dumped in this area. The precise nature of this monument is uncertain. While the whole does not appear to be natural, the stones are very rough and uneven. This may have been a folly erected as part of the landscaping of the former demense and cannot be classified conclusively as a portal tomb. (Tighe 1802, 625; Lewis 1837, vol. 2, 671; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 410-11).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly and Paul Walsh
Date of revised upload: 12 May 2021
KK013-061----:
On floor of small NW-SE valley. According to Carrigan (1905, vol. 3, 497) this standing stone was known as the ''Sthooic-Rawhaeola' [stook of Rathealy] or pointed rock of Rathealy', 'a pillar stone, 7 feet [2.1m] high, a few hundred yards east of the church [KK013-060001-]. It is said to have been thrown here all the way from Slievenamon by one of the old Irish giants'.
The standing stone (L 2.7m; 0.5m by 0.3m) originally stood in a field c. 230m SW of its present location (KK013-145----). At some stage it was moved up near the farmyard, then moved again to facilitate the construction of a silage dump (OPW files). It had been leaning against a tree in the farmyard before being placed upright in its present location.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 20 July 2015
KK021-029----:
At the foot of a steep slope 100m W of the River Barrow. Much of the monument is concealed beneath field debris that has been dumped there in modern times. The tomb (H 2.5m), aligned N-S, is very ruined and only one upright is now visible. A photo of the monument in the Bord Fáile archives shows a stone standing at the N end of gallery which has a gable-shaped backstone at its S end. The monument cannot be classified with certainty but appears to be related to the court/portal tomb traditions. (Prendergast 1967, 91; O'Kelly 1969, 77)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021
KK023-008----:
The OS Letters (1839) describe, 'In the Townland of Knockaliagain, i.e., the Hill of the Standing Stone, is a large rock reclining against a wall or ditch, measuring seven and a half feet [2.27m] in height over ground, two feet ten inches [0.87m] in breadth at bottom, one and a half feet [0.45m] at top and one foot [0.3m] in thickness' (O'Flanagan 1930, vol. 1, 267 (90)). O'Kelly (1969, 179) describes it as, 'The liagán, an uncarved and uninscribed land-stone column'.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 1 June 2021
KK024-024----:
Indicated as a circular enclosure on the 1st (1839) ed. OS 6-inch map and as a circular depression with trees in the interior on the revision. Subsequently levelled, the monument is visible as a well-defined cropmark on an aerial photographs (CUCAP AVL081, 15 July 1968; AYK074, 9 July 1969; BGH004 and 005, 16 July 1971). The circular enclosure (diam. c. 50m) is defined by a wide deep inner fosse and broad outer bank which is further enclosed by a slot trench (Gibbons 1990, 7). There is a possible single entrance in the E.
See attached:
KK024-024----_01 aerial photograph (CUCAP BGH004, 16 July 1971)
KK024-024----_02 aerial photograph (CUCAP AYK074, 9 July 1969)
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout
Date of upload: 2 February 2012
KK028-099----:
On an E-facing slope in a broadleaf plantation. A triangular sandstone slab (H 0.98m; Wth 0.36m; D 0.22m) oriented NNE-SSW in the centre of a mound (KK028-100----). There is a shallow depression (diam. c. 3m) around the base of the stone.
Compiled by: Mary Tunney
Date of upload: 23 October 2013
KK029-043----:
An upright stone, possibly a standing stone identified on an aerial photograph (ASIAP (56) 2-3, August 1996). The stone is indicated on both the 1st and 2nd ed. OS 6-inch map as ‘Barnastick’.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 1 September 2015
KK031-031----:
On a level shoulder of a NE facing slope. In 1983 the monument consisted of two portal stones (max. H 2.1m and 1.6m) which leaned markedly to the SE and indicated a chamber opening uphill to the SW. A roofstone (dims. 2.55m x 2.25m; T 0.45m) stood on edge against the E portal. This side of the monument was incorporated in a low fence. This has since been reclaimed and the stones moved out of position. (Ó Nualláin 1983, 97, no. 1)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021
KK031-112----:
Visible on satellite imagery (Tailte Éireann, satellite imagery 2011-2013 Digital Globe) and on Google Earth Street View, imagery date April 2009). There is a ritual pond (KK031-111----) c. 120m to the SE, a standing stone (KK031-113----) c. 470m to the E and a ring-barrow (KK035-007----) lies c. 1.3km to the SE.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
KK031-113----:
On a W-facing slope, in pasture. There are very good views to from SSW-W of Slievenamon Mountain and panoramic views from NW-NNE. The view from NE-SSW is impeded by surrounding hills slopes. A ritual pond (KK031-111----) is located c. 320m to the WSW and another standing stone (KK031-112----) is located c. 470m to the W. There is a ring-barrow (KK035-007----) c. 880m to the SE.
A roughly rectangular standing stone (0.55m x 0.18m; H 1.25m) orientated N-S. According to the landowner the stone was knocked over by a bull c. 10 years ago (c. 2014) and re-erected by the landowner in the exact position it had been previously. Only c. 0.1m of the stone had been embedded in the ground before it was knocked over. There is a hollow depression around the base of the standing stone where it has been trampled by cattle, using the stone as a scratching post.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
KK032-009001-:
In flat pasture at the W foot of Jerpoint Hill ridge about 500m E of the Little Arrigle River. The portal tomb was destroyed between 1850 and 1868. A sketch of the partly ruined monument by Rev. J. Graves (1850, facing 130) shows it as comprising a displaced roofstone, (dims. 3.65m x 2.6m; T 0.9m), resting against two portal stones and a door-stone. A number of other large slabs lay immediately beside the monument. This megalithic tomb is not visible at ground level.  (Graves 1850, 130; du Noyer 1868, 43; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 403, Knocktopher no. 1; Ó Nualláin 1983, 97, no. 2).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021
KK032-010----:
On the W-facing slope of the Jerpoint Hill ridge about 1.3 km SSW of a destroyed portal tomb (KK032-009001-). The monument stands immediately E of an old trackway to the rear of the outbuildings of an abandoned farmstead and was converted for use as an animal pen. It comprises a polygonal chamber (Wth c. 2m), whose sides, with the exception of two transversely-set portal-like orthostats at the N, are composed of modern dry-stone walling. There are two orthostats (H c. 1m), the W stone leans outwards. There is a modern opening through the dry-walling on the W. The whole is covered by a roofstone (dims.  3.8m x 2.05m; T 0.55m), that rests on the orthostats and dry-stone walling. A field-wall abuts the tomb at the N and S. (Graves 1850, 130; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 403, Knocktopher no. 2).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021

KK034-019001-:
National Monument No. 655.
On a gentle W facing slope, 120m E of the Lingaun River, surrounded by pasture. There are very good views of hills to the SE-S-SW and of Slievenamon to the W, with Baunfree passage tomb (KK034-031----) on Kilmacoliver Hill being visible 3.6km to the SSE and the cairn (TS078-001----) on Slivevenamon being visible 11km to the WSW. The monument is described by Carrigan (1905, vol. 4, 324-5), who mentions a lane cutting across the centre of the ‘Coshel’. It is described by Ó Nualláin and Cody (1987, vol. 117, 71-4) as a roughly circular, though quite overgrown, mound (diam. 27m; H 0.7-1m), defined by kerbstones, with two passages, one in the SW (L 3.5m; Wth at entrance 0.2m widening to 1m at rear), consisting of 12 orthostats, and the other smaller passage in the SE. Decoration on some of the kerbstones and on the orthostats of the SW tomb was noted (ibid., 71). Between 1990 and 1995 four seasons of archaeological excavation (Licence No. E000554) were carried out (O'Sullivan 1991, 40; 1992, 31; 1993, vol. 123, 5-18; 1995, 49-50; 1996, 51). It was found that the cairn was constructed on top of a raised earthen platform, which was created by scarping the slope (O’Sullivan 1993, vol. 123, 9). The cairn material was composed of three layers, the lower consisting of boulders (avg. diam. 0.3-0.4m) embedded in a dark reddish-purple soil which was overlaid by a layer of smaller stones (O’Sullivan 2011, No. 53). Over this lies a top layer of small stones which appear to be the result of relatively modern field clearance activity (ibid.). The SW tomb, which has a curving entrance façade, is larger and more elaborate than the SE tomb, having sophisticated decoration on many of its orthostats, as well as being aligned with the setting sun of the mid-Winter solstice (ibid.). The SE tomb was fully revealed during the excavations and it became evident that, unlike the SW tomb, this cruciform tomb (L 2.9m; Wth 2.2m) never had a passage extending to the edge of the kerbing of the mound (O’Sullivan 1993, vol. 123, 9). Also, only two of the orthostats of the SE tomb are decorated (ibid.). During the excavations considerable quantities of cremated bone were recovered from both tombs, though especially the SW tomb, as well as bone and antler pins, beads and pendants (ibid.). The lower part of a Carrowkeel Bowl and sherds of other Neolithic vessels were recovered from the SE tomb (ibid.). Fragments of Beaker pottery were recovered between the SE tomb and the kerbstones and a Food Vessel was found in the SW tomb (ibid.). The passage tomb art on the orthostats and kerbstones is described in detail by O’Sullivan (1987, vol. 117, 84-95).
See attached drawings of the passage-tomb art taken from O'Sullivan 1987.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 17 November 2017
KK034-031----:
Described by Ó Nualláin and Cody (1987, 74-6) as consisting of, 'a ruined megalithic chamber within a circular orthostatic kerb, concentric to and just inside which there are seven stones of what may have been an inner kerb, all on a grass-grown round mound. The northern outline of the mound is obscured by a length of field bank abutting it which was left undisturbed during land clearance. The mound measures 23.5m east-west and was perhaps a little in excess of that in the north-south direction. It is approximately lm high and extends from 3m to 6m beyond the kerb, the greater distance at the west which is slightly downhill from the site. Though grass-grown, it is felt to be stony and somewhat uneven underfoot. A more markedly uneven surface close to where it abuts the west end of the field bank might have been caused by heaping land clearance spoil here, though this is not certain.
Thirty stones (hatched on plan) of the encircling kerb survive in situ and define a space 14m to 15m in diameter. Though there are now notable gaps in the kerb at the west, south-west and north, and lesser ones elsewhere, it does seem that the close-spaced stones of the intact run at the south most closely resembles the original state of the monument. There is a doubling of the kerb at the south-west effected by placing a single stone outside and overlapping two others.
The original extent of the inner setting is not known. Five of the seven stones are set end-to-end at the south-east, another is 4m to the north and the seventh isolated at the north-west. They are 0.5m to 1.2m inside the encircling kerb and on a circumference which encloses a space approximately 11m in diameter.  These outer and inner stones vary in height from as low as 0.2m to a maximum of 1.35m, the height, if it was not leaning somewhat to the south, of the middle of an isolated group of three contiguous set stones at the west. The stones along the approximate eastern half of the kerb are generally lower than those of the remainder.
There is a sunken oval ring on the south face of the kerbstone that stands immediately alongside the single representative of the inner setting at the north-west. The ring is ill-defined, measures some 12cms across and is 1cm deep. While it may be artificially derived it is not possible to say if it is an original feature.  The megalithic chamber is in the western half of the kerbed circle and some three to four metres from its circumference. Rectangular in plan, it measures approximately 2m north-south and 1-3m east-west. Six stones of the chamber are still in situ. At the east there is a large orthostat 2.lm long. 0.3m thick and 0.45m high. At right angles to its southern end there are two set stones, jamb-like in appearance. 0.25m apart, the more easterly of the two 0.75m by 0.6m and 0.4m high, and the western 0.5m by 0.35m and  0.3m high. Leaning against the southern face of the eastern of the two and touching the east face of the western is a large slab, one end embedded in the ground, measuring 1.5m by 0.7m by 0.23m thick; it would seem that this has been displaced. …
KK034-032012-:
On the lower S-facing slope of Kilmacoliver Hill, overlooking the valley of the River Suir. Within Kilkieran graveyard (KK034-032002-), 2m N of the E end of an open-sided stone-walled rectangular grave-plot. The graveyard is located on the site of an early medieval monastery, as evidenced by four high crosses (KK034-032004-; KK034-032005-; KK034-032006-; KK034-032007-) within the graveyard. A conglomerate sandstone standing stone (H 0.77m; Wth at base 0.4m; tapering to 0.25) with pebble inclusions. The stone appears to be dressed to form a rounded profile at the top.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 20 August 2018

KK035-044----:
On the lower SE slopes of Carricktriss Gorse hill, adjacent to a small stream which flows S and eastward into Pollanassa River, in pasture. There are good views to the S. A standing stone (KK035-116----) is located c. 100m to the SW. The tomb is indicated on the 1st ed. OS map as ‘Leac an Scáil’, and versions of the name have appeared in various publications. Tighe (1802, 624) refers to it incorrectly as ‘Lachan Scahl (the Great Altar Stone)’, Borlase (1897, 405-07) gives the meaning for ‘Scal’ as a champion while Carrigan (1905, vol. 4, 248) translates it as ‘Rock of the Hero’.
The portal tomb is orientated NE-SW. It consists of a massive high-pitched capstone (max. dims. 5m by 3.2m; T 0.54m) which rests on a lower roofstone (max. dims. 2.41m by 1.85m; T 0.28m) and two portal stones (E stone 2.21m x 0.64m; H 3.59m; W stone 1.65m x 0.55m; H 3.55m). The two portal stones, the tallest stones in the tomb, form the entrance to a stone-lined burial chamber (E stone 3m x 0.3-0.43m; H 1.12m; W stone 1.9m x 0.9m; H 1.87m; S back stone 1.22m x 0.19m; H 1.62m; N sill stone 1.87m x 0.67m; H 3.08m). There are traces of a low retaining cairn along the E side of the monument but there is no visible trace of the encircling 'embankment, or rath' which, according to Borlase, formerly surrounded it (1897, vol. 2, 407).
(National Monument no. 324)
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 20 August 2018
KK035-053----:
On the E side and near the mouth of the narrow river valley that runs between the two hills N of Owning. Comprising a ruined chamber facing SSE represented by a broken W portal, a door-stone, the W sidestone and a leaning-in backstone. The E portal is prostate and the adjoining E sidestone is displaced. The roofstone (L 2.9m; Wth 2.5m; T 0.5m), has been dislodged to the W and its upper end rests on the backstone and W sidestone. A large slab beside the tomb to the S may be the broken upper portion of the W portal. Fogarty records that the monument was intact until c. 1825-30 and that the roofstone 'rested level on 7 large flags' (c. 1850, 21, 54). (Fogarty c. 1850, 21, 54; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 408,  Iverk no. 3; Powell 1941, 22, no. 25; Ó Nualláin 1983, 97, no. 3)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021

KK035-082----:
This was listed in the SMR (1987) as a ‘megalithic structure possible’. The source of this classification is a feature named ‘Stone’ on the first edition of the OS 6-inch map (1839). The name is not represented in the Gothic-style font used at that time to denote antiquities. This ‘Stone’ was not recorded on any subsequent OS map and no visible trace of this ‘Stone’ survived when the site was inspected in 1989. While the classification assigned to this record in the SMR (1987) could be taken to infer that this formed part of a possible ‘megalithic structure’ and the connotations that this implies, the evidence is not sufficient to warrant accepting it as such. The name ‘Stone’ suggests a single upright and this may be a standing stone (see KK038-008----) though this does not necessarily indicate that it is of any great antiquity.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 19 April 2023

KK035-096----:
Approximately 7m N of a motte (KK035-038----) on a level shoulder on the E side and at the head of a narrow river valley that runs between the two hills N of Owning. Carrigan (1905, vol. 2, 249) describes it as being '17ft. [c. 5m] long and about 3ft. [c. 0.9m] wide. Some of the stones are in situ, others fallen, but lying as they fell. . . now generally called the "Giant's Grave"'. The monument was destroyed between 1974 and 1982. Only an E end stone and adjoining N sidestone of a gallery remained in 1974. Two orthostats stood immediately N of this and formed a doubling of the gallery wall. It would seem probable that the monument was a megalithic tomb and interpretation of the remains as the E end of a wedge tomb gallery would not be inconsistent with the evidence. (Prendergast 1967, 91; O'Kelly 1969, 132 (under Curraghmore))
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021

KK035-112----:
In a shallow hollow on a broad shoulder of the N slope of Carricktriss hill. The W end of the monument is incorporated at an angle in a fence that runs along the N side of a farm lane. The remains comprise a gallery (L c. 5.1m), opening to the WNW. Its N side is composed of three stones and the S side of four stones; the W stone of the latter side is displaced and protrudes slightly through the fence where its base is visible. The E end of the gallery is closed by a backstone. This end is covered by a single roofstone which partly rests on a small orthostat that stands within the gallery just N of its S side. The exact function of this stone is uncertain. A second displaced roofstone lies on the S gallery wall that forms part of the fence. To the E of the backstone and in line with the gallery sides are two further orthostats which appear to indicate an end chamber (L c. 0.7m), open to the E. The S sidestone of this chamber is partly displaced and leans markedly inwards. Slight traces of a possible mound are visible to the N of the gallery and modern field clearance has been dumped against the fence at its SE end. Fogarty records that it was 'lately [dug] by gold dreamers. It was filled with black earth, charcoal, burned bones etc.' (Fogarty c. 1850, 85). (Ryan 1991, 883-4)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021

KK035-116----:
In pasture, on gentle SW-facing slope. This conglomerate upright (H 1.55m; Wth 1.35m; T 0.6m), oriented NW-SE, is firmly set in ground with some packing stones at base on SE-side. It is slightly narrower at the base and the width increases towards the top of the stone. Some loose field clearance stones have been placed near it. The portal tomb (KK035-044----) stands c. 100m to the NE.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 7 April 2017

KK036-035----:
Three granite stones, aligned N - S and set 1.2 - 1.7m apart. The stones decrease in height from S to N. The S stone measures 1.35m high is 0.85m W and 0.4m T. The middle stone is 1.25m high, 0.7m wide and 0.5m T. The N stone is 1.1m high, 0.6m wide and 0.5m T. This stone fell in 2012 and was re-erected in 2015 when the stones were painted white (Munster Expresss, 24 February 2015, page. 10). In 1849 the Rev. P. Moore recorded they were 'vulgarly termed "the three friars" a name derived, so far as he could conjecture, from no connection with the burial of friars, or from any such having suffered death there, but from these stones having been grouped together in mute and fraternal companionship.' (Moore 1849, 28). This story has been developed further in local lore and they are now considered to mark the place where three monks were murdered by the Cromwellians in 1651.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 27 February 2015
KK036-051----:
Close to the summit of a low hill (192m) overlooking the Black Water valley to the SW. The monument is ruined and has been partly dug out and disturbed. It consists of the remains of a gallery (L 5.2m; Wth 1m narrowing to 0.7m at E). The N side is formed of four orthostats including one transversely-set stone near the W end. Only two orthostats remain of the S side. To the S of the W of these are two buttress stones. There is a noticeable decrease in height of the gallery walls from W to E. Four outer-wall stones survive to the N of the gallery; one is almost prostrate. The area between the outer-wall and gallery side is filled with stones among which it is possible to distinguish a buttress-stone towards the W end. Two displaced slabs lie immediately W of the gallery. There is some evidence for mound to the N and S of the tomb though much of it appears to be covered by field debris and material thrown out from the earlier diggings at the monument. The gallery was formerly covered with roofstones but these were removed in the earlier 19th century (Cody 1851, 386; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 405, Knocktopher no. 6).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021

KK038-005----:
On a level shoulder on the E slope of the Lingaun river valley. The monument is very ruined and comprises a roofstone (L 3.75m; Wth 3m; T 0.9m), resting above a displaced orthostat, probably a sidestone. Modern field debris has been dumped around it. Fogarty records that it 'stood on 4 pillars about 3 foot [c. 0.9m]above ground' (c. 1850, 1). (Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 409, Iverk no. 7; Carrigan 1905, vol. 4, 247; Mason 1814, 364; Fogarty c. 1850, 1; Powell 1941, 22, no. 28; Ó Nualláin 1983, 97, no. 6)

KK038-009----:
In rolling farmland that slopes gently to the SW to a tributary stream of the Pill River. The tomb is partly incorporated in a fence on the N side of a lane. The remains comprise a ruined chamber facing N, represented by two portal stones (H 1.7m) and a door-stone; the W portal leans markedly outwards. A single W sidestone, also leaning outwards, stands beside it to the S. Its S end is partly embedded in the trunk of a tree. The large roofstone (L 5m; Wth 3.5m; T 0.7m), rests on the door-stone and E portal. There is no evidence for a surrounding cairn or mound. It may be concealed beneath the field clearance that has been dumped on either side of the monument. (Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 408, Iverk no. 5; Carrigan 1905, 247; Powell 1941, 22, no. 27; Ó Nualláin 1983, 98, no. 7)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021

KK039-044----:
In an old copse on the E side of a valley opening to the SW. It comprises a small ruined chamber (L c. 1.8m; Wth 1m), facing uphill to ENE. The entrance is formed by the N portal stone and a doorstone. The S portal has fallen outwards to the E and the S sidestone, in two pieces, leans inwards against the door-stone. The N sidestone is missing and a low line of crude dry-walling marks the edge of the chamber on this side. The W end is closed by two slabs which lean to the S; the N stone is split in two pieces. The roofstone (L 3.9m; Wth 1.9m; T 0.55m), has been displaced to the S and rests against the sidestone, door-stone and end slabs. The interior floor-level of the chamber is 2m below the capstone. There is no visible trace of a surrounding mound. (Borlase 1897, vol. 2, no. 409, Iverk no. 8; Powell 1941, 22, no. 26)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021
KK039-064----:
Approximately 40m W of a stream that flows S through a steep-sided valley. The monument is very ruined. It consists of a chamber (L at least 2.5m) opening to the NE. Only the W portal, leaning out markedly, and two adjoining sidestones are in situ. The chamber was covered by two roofstones. The N or upper stone is shattered into at least three pieces and lies tilted to the E. Fogarty (c. 1850, 103) records that it was blasted by powder. It partly rests above the S roofstone. This stands at an angle in the chamber and rests on and oversails the two sidestones. The whole E side of the monument is missing though a possible fallen sidestone protrudes from under the roofstones at the S. A 19th-century sketch of the monument from the NE depicts a leaning out door-stone and shows the N roofstone as intact (NLI 1356TA). (NLI 1356TA; Fogarty c. 1850, 103; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 409, Iverk no. 9; Powell 1941, 22, no. 29)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021

KK040-002001-:
On a gentle slope on the E side of the Black Water river valley. Named 'Large Grave' on the OS manuscript fair plan and described in the OS Letters (1839) as being 'twelve feet [3.65m] long and four [1.2m] wide. It was originally enclosed by a fence (lines) of large standing stones, three of which remain on the north side about the middle, one on the south side and one at the east end. They vary from three [0.9m] to four [1.2m] feet in height, inclining very much inwards.' (O'Flanagan 1930, vol. 2, 145). The account would appear to describe the remains of a ruined megalithic gallery. The monument appears to have been destroyed shortly after this description was written as it is not referred to in the mid-19th-century accounts of the monuments of this area (Anon. 1849, 27-8; Cody 1851, 385). (O'Flanagan 1930, vol. 2, 145; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 405, Knocktopher no. 5; Powell 1941, 22, no. 31).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021
KK040-020001-:
On the NE flank of Tory Hill on the W side of a shallow valley, within an overgrown triangular area (Wth 22m at SW) of uncultivated land. Consisting of two very ruined back-to-back galleries (L c. 15m), aligned NE - SW. Each gallery appears to have been divided into two chambers. The SW gallery is 5m long and its front portion is destroyed. The rear chamber is represented by a gable-shaped backstone, two sidestones and two opposing, inset jamb-stones. There is a single surviving N sidestone of the second chamber to the SW. Beyond this a field bank crosses the monument. The NE gallery (L 6m) is more disturbed but was of similar construction to the other. The rear chamber is represented by the backstone, a single N sidestone and two opposing, inset jambs-stones. Only two stones of the N side of the chamber to the NE survive. The outermost may be a longitudinally-set entrance jamb or portal. A distance of 1.7m separates the backstones of the galleries. Though no evidence of a court survives the general design is clearly indicative of the monument being the remains of a dual court tomb. (de Valéra and Ó Nualláin 1962, 117-23)
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021
KK040-037----:
On rough pasture at the head of the shallow valley of a stream that runs N to the Arrigle River. It comprises a ruined gallery (L c. 4m; av. Wth 1m), aligned E - W. Four stones form the S side and there are three on the N. The W stone of the latter is displaced and appears to have been deliberately shattered. Two other loose slabs lie at this end of the gallery which appears to have been dug out. A doubling of the gallery wall is suggested by a single stone immediately outside its N side and there is a buttress-like stone outside the S side of the gallery. Traces of an enclosing mound survive on the N, W and S sides. Though the orientation and some of the structural details are suggestive of it being a wedge tomb the monument is best left unclassified. (Moore 1849, 12; Borlase 1897, vol. 2, 405, Knocktopher no. 7; Powell 1941, 22, no. 32).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 10 May 2021

KK042-050----:
On a gentle slope on the W side of a broad, shallow valley that opens to the S. A fence to the S of the monument was removed in the early 1990s and the remains, together with other field debris, are piled on the monument. The tomb consists of a small chamber (L at least c. 1.3m; Wth c. 1m), aligned NNE - SSW. The W sidestone is split in two pieces. Its E counterpart is not parallel to it but is slightly skewed. It was formerly roofed by a large roofstone (L c. 3m long; Wth 2.4m; T 0.27m) (Fogarty c. 1850, 88). The remaining N portion rests at an angle against the S ends of the sidestones. Fogarty (ibid. 89) records that it 'was surrounded formerly by a circle of pillars, but there is nothing remaining'. The monument is known locally as a reputed mass-rock.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021
KK043-060----:
On the NW side of Airmount crossroads, on almost level ground. There are good views to the W over the low-lying Suir Valley and to the Comeraghs. The stones are known locally as 'The Three Friars' (Carrigan 1905, vol. 4, 202). The group consists of three conglomerate standing stones, the largest incorporated into a field wall, with the other two standing stones c. 60m to the NW.  The largest stone (H 1.85m; Wth 1.05m by 0.7m) leans to the SW. The smallest stone (H 1.25m; L 1m; W 0.35m) aligned NW-SE and the third stone (H 1.5m; Wth 0.7m by 0.6m) which was 12m NE of the smallest, aligned NW-ESE. The standing stones were excavated and re-located in 2003 to facilitate the construction of the N25 Waterford Bypass (Wren 2006, 276-7). All three stones had been set into sockets cut into the natural boulder clay. The smallest stone (total H 1.45m) had a circle of twelve post-holes surrounding it (ibid.). Testing had revealed the remains of a possible cist burial at the base of the third stone (ibid.).  Immediately N of this stone there was a square cut in the natural boulder clay which was interpreted as possibly a socket for a fourth stone (ibid.). This socket was cut on the N side by an oval pit, the vertical sides and base of which were lined with limestone, forming a polygonal cist, with a split red sandstone capstone (ibid.). A fourth conglomerate stone (H 0.79m; Wth 0.68m; T 0.43m tapering to 0.14m), lying prostrate, may have been part of the group but excavation revealed no socket where it was lying (ibid.).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 29 March 2017

KK043-100----:
On level ground c. 20m S of a river, in a small river valley, in rough pasture. On the 1st (1840) ed. OS 6-inch map the river is indicated as a mill race with a flour mill and mill pond c. 90m to the E. There are also a number of buildings indicated in the vicinity on the 1st and revised edition of the 6-inch OS map but these are no longer upstanding. There is a sheer rock face c. 20m to the S and a road with a bridge over the river c. 30m to the W. The views are limited in all directions. A grey conglomerate standing stone (H 2.2m) with some small pebbles visible in its composition. The stone is rectangular in plan (Wth 1.04m tapering to 0.47m at top on SW side; 1m tapering to 0.43m at top on NE side; 0.45m tapering to 0.24m at top on NW side; 0.35m widening slightly to 0.4m at top on SE side) and tapers towards the top, with its long axis orientated NW-SE. There is a slight outward bulge (H 0.3m) on the NE side, c. 0.9m above ground level. The top surface of the standing stone is flat but sloping, with the highest point on the SE side sloping down to the NW, the surface also slopes from NE to SW. There are no visible packing stones around the base.

Compiled by: Jean Farrelly

KK045-015----:
On the shoulder of a SE facing slope overlooking the River Suir. There are two different descriptions of this monument from the mid-19th century. It was reported in 1849 as being 'twenty-five feet [7.62m] long, and ten or twelve [3.05m or 3.66m] wide . . . The grave was lined with huge flags, and at the head and foot were enormous stones about sixteen feet [4.88m] in height' and that it was opened c. 1790 when a 'gigantic skeleton, with a huge sword, much rust-eaten . . . [and] a helmet of uncommon size' were found (Moore 1849, 13). In 1852 it was described as 'consisting of a cist or cavity about eight feet [2.44m] long, three feet [91cm] deep, and three feet [91cm] wide. A pile of stone now occupies the “narrow bed” of the hero, which bears about one point north-east, and from the position of four upright stones still remaining, it appears to have been surrounded by a row of such stones disposed in circular order, and enclosing an area of about twelve feet [3.66m] in diameter.' (Cody 1852, 101). According to local information the monument was destroyed about thirty years ago [c. 1960s] in the course of land reclamation. The exact nature of this site is uncertain and it cannot be classified with certainty as a megalithic tomb.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 12 May 2021

On an E-facing slope of a N-S valley. A rectangular stone of Old Red Sandstone conglomerate (dims 1.2m x 0.5m) is oriented ENE-WSW and has a broken top which achieves its maximum height (H 1.2m) at the E end.
